Butter madeleine tins, fill them two-thirds, and bake at 200°C until the humps set and the edges gold.
Unmould at once.
Eat the same day; they stale overnight.

title: Mont-Blanc chestnut cream
description: Sweet chestnut purée piped over whipped cream, looking like vermicelli snow on a mountain.
notes: A potato ricer makes the classic vermicelli if you lack a piping nozzle.
steps: Simmer chestnuts with milk and sugar until very soft, then mash or mill into a paste.
Whip cream with vanilla to soft peaks.
Spoon cream into dishes and pipe chestnut paste in thin strands over the top.
Chill 20 minutes so the strands set.
Serve cold; it is rich, so keep portions modest.

title: Choucroute garnie
description: Alsatian sauerkraut simmered with sausages, pork and juniper — a winter feast plate.
notes: Riesling in the pot is traditional; any dry white works.
steps: Rinse sauerkraut if very salty, then simmer with juniper, apple and wine for an hour.
Nestle smoked pork in the cabbage and continue until tender.
Brown sausages separately and add for the last 20 minutes.
Pile cabbage on a platter and arrange the meats on top.
Serve with boiled potatoes, not sauceboats.

title: Aligot
description: Mashed potato beaten with tomme cheese until it stretches in ribbons — a mountain side for roast meats.
notes: Mozzarella plus a little cheddar is a rough stand-in for tomme.
steps: Boil potatoes, mash with butter, milk, garlic and salt until smooth.
Over low heat, beat in diced tomme until the mash turns elastic and glossy.
Lift with a spoon; it should form long ribbons.
Serve immediately; aligot waits for no one.
If it tightens, beat in a splash more hot milk.

title: Kir royal
description: Crème de cassis in the bottom of a flute, topped with sparkling wine for a réveillon toast.
notes: Use a dry sparkling wine; sweet bubbles plus cassis cloy.
steps: Pour a spoon of cassis into each chilled flute.
Top slowly with sparkling wine so the drink does not foam over.
Drop in a raspberry and a hint of lemon zest if you like perfume.
Stir once with a spoon stem.
Mix to order; a jug of kir royal goes flat.

title: Kougelhopf
description: An Alsatian yeasted cake baked in a fluted tin with raisins and almonds, sliced for Christmas breakfast.
notes: A bundt tin works if you lack the traditional mould.
steps: Make a yeast dough with flour, milk, butter, eggs and yeast; knead in raisins.
Butter a kougelhopf tin, stud with almonds, and fill halfway.
Rise until the dough nears the rim.
Bake at 170°C until gold and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool five minutes, then turn out and dust with sugar.

title: Endives au jambon
description: Braised chicory wrapped in ham and baked under cheese sauce — a northern family gratin for winter.
notes: Squeezing the braised endives is the unglamorous secret.
steps: Braise endives in a covered pan until tender; drain well so the gratin does not water.
Wrap each in ham and lay in a dish.
Make a white sauce with butter, flour and milk, add most of the gruyère, and pour over.
Scatter remaining cheese and bake at 190°C until bubbling.
Rest five minutes before serving.

title: Saumon en croûte
description: A side of salmon in puff pastry with a herbed filling, baked until the pastry is gold and the fish just flakes.
notes: Pat the salmon very dry or the pastry base sogs.
steps: Wilt spinach, squeeze dry, and mix with cream cheese and dill.
Sit the salmon on pastry, top with the spinach mix, and wrap, sealing with beaten egg.
Egg-wash, slash the top, and bake at 200°C until the pastry is deep gold.
Rest 10 minutes; the fish carries on cooking.
Slice with a serrated knife so the pastry does not crush.

title: Pot-au-feu
description: A family boiled dinner of beef and winter vegetables, served with mustard and coarse salt.
notes: Keep the simmer lazy; boiling clouds the broth and toughens shin.
steps: Cover beef with water, bring to a simmer, and skim.
Add salt and cook until the meat is yielding, about two hours.
Add leeks, carrots and potatoes and cook until the vegetables are tender.
Serve broth in cups, then the meat and vegetables with mustard and salt.
Marrow bones in the pot are a bonus if the butcher has them.

title: Mousse au chocolat
description: Dark chocolate folded with whipped egg so the mousse sets airy and bitter-sweet in glasses.
notes: Use chocolate you like to eat; the mousse tastes exactly of it.
steps: Melt chocolate with butter; cool until tepid.
Beat yolks in, then fold in whites whipped with sugar and salt to stiff peaks.
Spoon into glasses and chill at least two hours.
Serve cold, unadorned or with a little cream.
Do not overfold or you lose the air.

title: Champagne cocktail
description: A sugar cube soaked with bitters in a flute, topped with champagne and a strip of lemon peel.
notes: A dry champagne works better than a sweet one here.
steps: Soak each sugar cube with bitters and drop it into a chilled flute.
Top with champagne so the cube fizzes from the bottom.
Twist lemon peel over the glass and drop it in.
Do not stir; the sugar dissolves as people drink.
Build each glass to order so the sugar still fizzes from the bottom.

title: Paper-cone roast chestnuts
description: Chestnuts scored and roasted until the skins split, served in a paper cone as a winter street snack at home.
notes: Old dry chestnuts stay hard; buy heavy, glossy ones.
steps: Score an X through each chestnut shell so they do not explode.
Toss with a spoon of water and salt, then roast at 200°C until the cuts peel back.
Wrap in a towel for five minutes so the skins steam loose.
Peel while warm and finish with pepper if you like.
Serve in a bowl or paper cone immediately.

title: Red-fruit yule roll
description: A lighter bûche: genoise rolled with raspberry cream rather than chocolate bark, for tables that already have a cocoa log.
notes: This is intentionally not a chocolate bûche; keep both on a large table if you want.
steps: Bake a thin genoise from eggs, sugar and flour; roll in a cloth while warm.
Whip cream with icing sugar and fold in crushed raspberries.
Unroll, spread the cream, and roll again.
Chill, then dust with icing sugar instead of chocolate coating.
Slice to show the pink spiral.

title: Réveillon crêpes au sucre
description: Thin Breton-style crêpes with butter and sugar, cooked at the table after a long réveillon.
notes: The batter should be as thin as cream; add milk if it sits thick.
steps: Whisk flour, milk, eggs and salt into a thin batter; rest 20 minutes.
Cook thin crêpes in a hot buttered pan, swirling to coat.
Sprinkle sugar and a little butter on each, fold into triangles.
Keep stacked under a cloth.
A squeeze of lemon is allowed for those who want sharpness.

title: Gratin de cardons
description: Cardoons simmered then baked in a pale sauce — a Lyonnais Christmas vegetable that tastes of artichoke and celery.
notes: Celery hearts are a rough substitute if cardoons are impossible to find.
steps: Peel cardoon stalks, cut into lengths, and simmer in lemony water until tender; drain hard.
Make a white sauce with butter, flour and milk.
Fold cardoons into the sauce, put in a dish, and cover with gruyère.
Bake at 190°C until the top browns.
Serve as a side to capon or dinde.

title: Escargots de Bourgogne
description: Snails baked in garlic-parsley butter until the butter roars in the shells.
notes: Use prepared snails in brine; foraging is not a réveillon activity.
steps: Beat butter with crushed garlic, chopped parsley and salt.
Tuck a snail and a knob of garlic butter into each shell or dish hollow.
Bake at 200°C until the butter is bubbling furiously.
Serve with baguette to mop the butter.
Protect hands; the dishes stay hotter than the snails.

title: Hazelnut praline bûche
description: A nut-forward yule log with praline buttercream, distinct from the cocoa bûche and the red-fruit roll.
notes: Keep this off the table if you already plated the cacao bûche for a small group; they compete.
steps: Bake a thin sponge from eggs, sugar and flour; roll and cool.
Toast hazelnuts, grind half with a little sugar into praline paste, chop the rest.
Beat butter with the praline paste and melted chocolate into a filling.
Spread, roll, coat, and press chopped hazelnuts along the sides.
Chill before slicing so the praline cream does not smear.

title: White vin chaud
description: Alsatian white wine warmed with orange, cinnamon and a little ginger — a paler market cup than red vin chaud.
notes: A dry Riesling or Pinot Blanc is the right base.
steps: Warm white wine with orange slices, sliced ginger, cinnamon, star anise and sugar.
Hold below a simmer 12 minutes.
Taste; white wine needs less sugar than red as a rule.
Strain into glasses.
Do not use an oaked chardonnay; it tastes clumsy when hot.

title: Pommes dauphine
description: Piped choux-potato puffs fried until they swell — a feast potato that is not a gratin and not a roast.
notes: The mix should be pipeable, not sloppy; add potato if it is wet.
steps: Mash dry boiled potatoes.
Make a small choux paste with water, butter and flour, beat in eggs, then mix with the potato and salt.
Fry spoonfuls in 170°C oil until they puff and gold.
Drain and salt at once.
Serve immediately; they deflate if they wait.

title: Mâche salad with walnuts
description: A sharp lamb's lettuce salad with walnuts and a mustard vinaigrette to cut réveillon richness.
notes: Dressing in the bowl first, leaves second, keeps the salad from pooling.
steps: Wash mâche carefully; it holds grit.
Whisk mustard with vinegar, then oil into a thick dressing.
Toss the leaves lightly so they do not collapse.
Scatter walnuts over the top rather than mixing them to mush.
Serve at once beside terrines or smoked fish.

title: Frozen nougat bûche
description: A moulded iced nougat log with candied fruit, sliced frozen — a bûche that never sees the oven.
notes: This is the make-ahead bûche when oven space is gone.
steps: Whip cream to soft peaks.
Cook honey, pour onto whipped egg whites to make a light nougat meringue, then fold in cream, chopped pistachios and peel.
Line a loaf tin, pack the mixture, and freeze overnight.
Turn out, slice with a hot knife, and serve still frozen.
A little extra honey on the plate is enough sauce.

title: Weihnachtsgans with apple and sage
description: A German Christmas goose stuffed with apple, onion and sage, roasted until the fat renders and the skin turns mahogany.
notes: Save every spoon of fat for potatoes and red cabbage.
steps: Prick the goose skin, salt it well, and stuff the cavity with apple, onion and sage.
Roast on a rack at 160°C, pouring off fat twice, until the thighs are 75°C.
Raise the heat to 220°C for 15 minutes to crisp the skin.
Rest 30 minutes before carving.
Serve the collapsed apples as a sharp spooning garnish.

title: Rotkohl with apple
description: German red cabbage braised with apple, vinegar and cloves until jammy enough to cut roast goose.
notes: A spoon of goose fat in the pot is traditional on meat days.
steps: Shred cabbage and slice apples.
Layer in a pot with sugar, salt, cloves and vinegar.
Cover and cook on low until the cabbage is silky, about an hour.
Uncover to reduce if watery.
Tastes better reheated the next day.

title: Semmelknödel
description: Bavarian bread dumplings poached until they bounce, served with goose gravy.
notes: A test dumpling tells you if the mix needs more bread or milk.
steps: Cube the rolls and soak with warm milk until they yield but are not soup.
Soften onion in butter, then mix with bread, eggs, parsley and salt.
Shape into balls with wet hands.
Poach in barely simmering water until they float and feel set, about 15 minutes.
Drain and serve at once; they firm as they cool.

title: Dresdner Stollen
description: A butter-rich Christmas loaf packed with raisins and candied peel, folded over and buried in icing sugar.
notes: Wrap and rest a week if you can; the crumb moistens.
steps: Soak raisins in a little water or rum; make a rich yeast dough with flour, milk, yeast and half the butter.
Knead in fruit, peel and chopped almonds; rise until puffy.
Shape into a flattened oval, fold one side two-thirds over, and rise again.
Bake at 170°C until the loaf is cooked through and gold.
Brush with remaining melted butter while hot and dredge heavily in icing sugar; repeat when cool.

title: Lebkuchen
description: Nuremberg-style honey-spice cookies, soft in the middle, often glazed or chocolate-dipped.
notes: Lebkuchen spice is cinnamon, clove, nutmeg and cardamom in equal curiosity.
steps: Warm honey, mix with flour, almonds, egg and spice into a sticky dough; rest overnight if you can.
Scoop mounds onto a tray and flatten slightly.
Bake at 170°C until set but still soft.
Cool, then dip in melted chocolate or brush with a thin sugar glaze.
Store in a tin; they soften and improve.

title: Glühwein
description: German market mulled wine with orange, cinnamon and clove, sweetened just enough to drink outdoors.
notes: Orange juice in the pan is a German market trick for body.
steps: Warm wine with orange juice, orange slices, cinnamon, cloves and sugar.
Hold at a steam for 15 minutes; never boil.
Taste for sugar; market Glühwein is sweeter than table wine.
Strain into mugs.
A shot of rum is optional for adults standing in snow.

title: Swabian warm potato salad
description: A warm potato salad dressed with broth and vinegar, no mayonnaise — the southern German Christmas roast companion.
notes: Mayonnaise versions are northern; this one is the roast-meat partner.
steps: Boil potatoes in skins until just tender; peel while warm and slice.
Warm broth with vinegar, oil, grated onion and salt.
Pour the dressing over the warm slices so they drink it.
Rest 20 minutes, then taste; it should be sharp and savoury.
Serve slightly warm beside goose or sausages.

title: Sauerbraten
description: Beef marinated in vinegar and spice, then braised until it slices into a sweet-sour gravy, sometimes finished with gingerbread.
notes: The marinade is the dish; do not skip the days in the fridge.
steps: Marinate the beef 2–3 days in vinegar, onion, cloves and bay, turning once a day.
Brown the drained joint, then braise in strained marinade until tender.
Crumble lebkuchen into the sauce to thicken and spice it.
Slice the beef and nap with gravy.
Serve with potato dumplings and rotkohl.

title: Zimtsterne
description: Cinnamon almond stars with a white meringue lid, baked just enough to set the icing.
notes: Low oven is essential; high heat yellows the stars.
steps: Mix almonds, most of the sugar, cinnamon and one egg white into a dough.
Roll between icing sugar, cut stars, and cap each with remaining egg white beaten with sugar.
Bake at 140°C until the icing sets but stays pale.
Cool on the tray.
They should be chewy, not crisp.

title: Spekulatius
description: Thin spiced biscuits pressed with windmill patterns, baked until they snap.
notes: Speculoos spice is cinnamon-heavy with clove and nutmeg.
steps: Beat butter and sugar, add egg, then flour, spice and soda; chill the dough.
Roll thin and press into a carved mould or cut rectangles.
Bake at 180°C until the edges brown and the biscuits smell toasted.
Cool on a rack so they crisp.
Store airtight; humidity kills the snap.

title: Pfeffernüsse
description: Peppery glazed spice cookies, small enough to eat by the handful with coffee.
notes: Make them a week ahead for the classic texture.
steps: Mix flour with honey, sugar, egg, pepper and cinnamon into a firm dough.
Roll small balls and bake at 170°C until set.
Toss warm cookies in a thin icing-sugar glaze, or dust when cool.
They harden as they cool, then soften in the tin.
White pepper is the point; black pepper is harsher.

title: Kartoffelklöße
description: Thuringian potato dumplings, sometimes with a toasted bread cube inside, poached until they lift.
notes: Too much flour makes cannonballs; add only until the mix holds.
steps: Boil half the potatoes, rice them, and grate the rest raw; squeeze the raw potato dry.
Combine with flour, salt and nutmeg.
Fry bread cubes in butter and hide one in each dumpling if you like the Thuringian surprise.
Poach in salted water until they float and feel bouncy.
Serve with goose gravy.

title: Eierpunsch
description: A German Christmas-market egg punch of white wine, citrus and yolk, served warm and foamy.
notes: A thermometer around 70°C keeps the eggs safe and silky.
steps: Whisk yolks with sugar until pale.
Warm wine, lemon zest and orange juice without boiling.
Whisk the hot wine into the yolks, return to a low heat, and stir until slightly thick; do not scramble.
Add rum off the heat.
Serve immediately in cups while the foam sits on top.

title: Bratapfel with marzipan
description: Whole apples stuffed with marzipan and raisins, baked until they slump and the skins wrinkle.
notes: Choose apples that hold shape; very soft eaters collapse into sauce.
steps: Core the apples without cutting through the base.
Stuff with chopped marzipan and raisins, and sit them in a dish with a little water.
Dot with butter and sugar.
Bake at 180°C until the apples are soft and the stuffing bubbles.
Serve with the pan juices; cream is optional.

title: Rumkugeln
description: Chocolate rum truffle balls rolled in sprinkles or cocoa, no baking, for the cookie plate.
notes: Cake crumbs can bulk them out if you have leftover sponge.
steps: Melt chocolate with butter, then beat in icing sugar and rum until thick.
Chill until scoopable.
Roll balls and coat in sprinkles.
Chill again to set.
Keep cool; they soften in a warm room.

title: Spätzle
description: Irregular egg noodles scraped into boiling water, tossed in butter — a Swabian side for sauerbraten.
notes: The batter should be thicker than pancake mix; rest five minutes.
steps: Beat flour, eggs, milk and salt into a thick, stretchy batter.
Push through a spätzle press or board into boiling salted water.
When they float, fish them out.
Toss in butter until glossy.
A handful of fried breadcrumbs on top is allowed.

title: Entenbraten with orange
description: Roast duck with orange and a little honey, a smaller German Christmas bird than goose.
notes: Duck is fattier than chicken; a rack over a tin is not optional.
steps: Prick the duck skin, salt it, and stuff with orange halves and thyme.
Roast at 180°C, pouring off fat, until the skin is crisp and the thighs cooked.
Brush honey mixed with orange juice on for the last 15 minutes.
Deglaze the tin with wine for a sharp jus.
Rest 20 minutes before carving.

title: Heringssalat
description: A northern German herring salad with beetroot and apple, pink and sharp, served on Christmas Eve.
notes: Wear an apron; beet stains everything.
steps: Dice herring, cooked beetroot, apple and onion into even cubes.
Fold with sour cream and salt.
Chill at least an hour so the beet colours everything.
Taste for sharpness; a little pickle brine helps.
Serve with bread as a starter or late supper.

title: Aachener Printen
description: Firm honey-spice rectangles from Aachen, sometimes chocolate-coated, meant to keep.
notes: Baking soda can stand in for potash in a home kitchen.
steps: Warm honey, mix with flour, spice, potash and chopped peel into a stiff dough; rest overnight.
Roll and cut rectangles.
Bake at 180°C until firm.
Cool, then dip in chocolate if you want the coated style.
They start hard and mellow in a tin.

title: Marzipankartoffeln
description: Marzipan rolled into potato shapes and dusted with cocoa — a playful German sweet-shop classic.
notes: Do not make them perfectly round or they look like truffles, not potatoes.
steps: Knead marzipan with a spoon of icing sugar until pliable.
Roll small irregular ovals like new potatoes.
Dust with cocoa mixed with cinnamon so they look earthy.
Let them dry an hour so the cocoa sticks.
Store cool; they dry out if left uncovered for days.

title: Feuerzangenbowle
description: Mulled wine with a rum-soaked sugar cone set alight so caramel drips into the bowl — a theatrical German party drink.
notes: This is theatre; for a quiet night, make Glühwein instead.
steps: Warm wine with orange, cinnamon and cloves in a fireproof bowl.
Rest the sugar cone on tongs over the bowl, soak it with rum, and ignite.
Ladle more rum over the burning sugar so caramel drips into the wine.
When the flame dies, stir and serve.
Keep a lid nearby and never leave the bowl unattended.

title: Nussecken
description: Hazelnut-topped shortbread triangles with chocolate-dipped corners.
notes: Cut while warm or the nut layer shatters.
steps: Press a short dough of flour, butter and some sugar into a tin and bake until just set.
Spread apricot jam, then a mix of chopped hazelnuts, remaining sugar and a little butter.
Bake until the nuts are toasted.
Cut into triangles while warm and dip two corners in melted chocolate.
Set on parchment until the chocolate hardens.

title: Springerle
description: Anise-scented white cookies stamped with moulds, dried until a 'foot' forms, then baked pale.
notes: Skipping the drying step loses the printed pattern.
steps: Beat eggs and sugar until very thick, then fold in flour, hartshorn, salt and anise.
Roll, press with springerle moulds, cut, and dry uncovered 12 hours so a skin forms.
Bake at 150°C until the bases have a little foot and the tops stay white.
Cool and store; the anise strengthens.
Baking powder can replace hartshorn with a slightly different rise.

title: Leberknödelsuppe
description: Liver dumplings in clear broth — a Bavarian first course before goose.
notes: Chicken liver works but is milder.
steps: Soak bread, squeeze it, and mix with minced liver, grated onion, egg and parsley.
Shape dumplings and poach in barely simmering broth until they float and are cooked through.
Serve two or three per bowl with the clear broth.
Do not boil hard or the dumplings toughen.
A grind of pepper at the table is enough.

title: Cranberry rotkohl
description: Red cabbage braised with cranberries instead of apple for a sharper vegan German side.
notes: Distinct from the apple rotkohl; serve one or the other.
steps: Shred cabbage and combine with cranberries, vinegar, sugar, salt and cinnamon.
Cook covered until the cabbage is soft and the berries have burst.
Reduce uncovered if the pan is wet.
The berries should stain the cabbage a deeper red than apple versions.
Reheat gently; it keeps three days.

title: Bavarian Vanillekipferl
description: Crescent almond biscuits rolled in vanilla sugar while warm — German-Austrian border baking.
notes: Czech vanilkové rohlíčky are cousins; this version uses more butter.
steps: Mix flour, butter, almonds and sugar into a dough; chill 30 minutes.
Shape small crescents and bake at 170°C until the undersides just colour.
Roll in vanilla sugar while still warm.
Cool completely before boxing.
They snap if overbaked; pale is correct.

title: Weißer Glühwein
description: White mulled wine with apple and vanilla, a market variant paler than classic Glühwein.
notes: A dry Pinot Blanc or Müller-Thurgau is a good base.
steps: Warm wine with apple juice, split vanilla, cinnamon, lemon peel and sugar.
Steep below a simmer 12 minutes.
Strain into mugs.
Do not boil or the white wine turns bitter.
Vanilla should be noticeable but not like dessert sauce.

title: Grünkohl with Pinkel
description: Northern German kale stew with oat sausage, a winter plate that often appears between Advent and New Year.
notes: Any smoked oat or pork sausage stands in if Pinkel is unavailable.
steps: Strip kale from stems, blanch, and chop.
Cook onion in lard, add kale and a little water, and simmer until the leaves are very tender.
Add potatoes and nestle Pinkel in the kale to heat through.
Season with salt; the sausage is already spiced.
Serve in deep plates with mustard.

title: Stollenkonfekt
description: Bite-size stollen cubes baked as confectionery rather than a loaf, useful for gifting.
notes: Easier than a full Dresden loaf when you want the flavour in a cookie box.
steps: Make a small enriched dough with flour, milk, yeast and some butter; knead in raisins and chopped almonds.
Rise, then roll into a slab and cut small rectangles.
Bake at 170°C until just gold.
Brush with remaining melted butter and toss in icing sugar.
They keep in a tin for a week.

title: Red-wine sauce for roast goose
description: A reduced red-wine sauce with stock and a little jelly, for goose or sauerbraten when pan juices are thin.
notes: Goose roasting juices can replace some of the stock.
steps: Soften shallot, add wine and thyme, and reduce by half.
Add stock and reduce until the sauce coats a spoon.
Whisk in jelly and butter off the heat.
Strain for a smooth jug.
Taste for salt; stock strength varies.

title: Lebkuchen house slabs
description: A sturdier lebkuchen dough baked as slabs for assembling a house, or eaten as thick spice biscuits.
notes: Bake extra slabs; corners break.
steps: Mix a stiff dough from flour, honey, sugar, egg, spice and soda; chill 30 minutes.
Roll 8 mm thick and cut wall and roof shapes, or simple rectangles.
Bake at 170°C until firm to the touch.
Cool completely before icing together if you are building.
Royal icing is the mortar; sweets are optional decoration.

title: Kartoffelpuffer with apple sauce
description: Crisp potato pancakes with apple sauce — a German winter plate children will actually eat.
notes: Squeeze harder than you think; water is the enemy of crust.
steps: Grate potatoes and onion, squeeze dry in a cloth.
Mix with eggs and salt.
Fry spoonfuls in oil until both sides are deep gold and crisp.
Drain the fried pieces on paper so the crust stays crisp rather than soggy.
Serve with apple sauce, not ketchup, if you can win that argument.

title: Dark-beer onion gravy
description: Onions caramelised and deglazed with dark beer into a gravy for knödel and roast meats.
notes: A malty dunkles works better than a bitter IPA.
steps: Cook onions in butter until brown and sweet.
Stir in flour, then beer and stock.
Simmer until the gravy thickens and the alcohol smell fades.
Season with salt.
Strain if you want it smooth, or leave the onions in.

title: Crisp goose legs
description: Goose legs roasted on their own for a small household that does not want a whole Weihnachtsgans.
notes: Much easier to cook evenly than a whole bird.
steps: Salt the legs overnight if you can, then pat dry.
Set on apple slices and sage in a tin, skin up.
Roast at 160°C until the meat is tender, then raise heat to crisp the skin.
Rest 10 minutes.
Spoon off fat for potatoes; serve the apples as a garnish.

title: Quarkstollen
description: A quicker stollen lightened with quark instead of a long butter dough, still buried in sugar.
notes: Not a Dresden yeast stollen; it is the weeknight cousin.
steps: Mix flour, baking powder, quark, egg and some butter into a dough; knead in raisins.
Shape into a folded stollen loaf.
Bake at 170°C until cooked through.
Brush with remaining melted butter and dredge with icing sugar.
Slice the next day; it cuts cleaner.

title: Barszcz wigilijny
description: Clear beetroot broth for Christmas Eve, ruby and sour, served with uszka or on its own.
notes: A piece of fermented beet kvass instead of vinegar is more traditional if you have it.
steps: Simmer beetroot, onion, bay, mushrooms and salt until the broth is deep red, about 90 minutes.
Strain through cloth so the soup is clear.
Sharpen with vinegar; it should taste sour and earthy, not like borscht stew.
Reheat without boiling so the colour stays bright.
Serve in cups with uszka floated in, or as a starter alone.

title: Uszka with mushrooms
description: Tiny ear-shaped dumplings stuffed with wild mushrooms, boiled and served in barszcz on Christmas Eve.
notes: Seal well; leaks cloud the clear broth.
steps: Soak mushrooms, then chop and cook with onion in oil until dry and dark.
Make a firm pasta dough with flour, egg, salt and water; rest it.
Roll thin, cut small squares, fill, and pinch into little ears.
Boil in salted water until they float plus a minute.
Serve a few in each bowl of barszcz; they should not crowd the soup.

title: Fried carp for Wigilia
description: Carp portions salted, floured and fried until the skin crisps — the Christmas Eve fish of many Polish tables.
notes: Ask the fishmonger to scale and clean it; home scaling is a war.
steps: Cut carp into portions, salt them, and rest 20 minutes; pat dry.
Dust with flour and fry in hot oil until both sides are gold and the flesh flakes.
Drain the fried pieces on paper so the crust stays crisp rather than soggy.
Serve with lemon and potato salad.
A quiet kitchen helps; carp pops in the pan.

title: Mushroom cutlets
description: Pan-fried cutlets of chopped mushrooms and breadcrumbs — a Wigilia main when the table skips carp.
notes: Dry pan work is essential; wet mushrooms will not bind.
steps: Chop mushrooms and onion finely and cook until all liquid is gone.
Cool, then mix with breadcrumbs, eggs and salt.
Shape cutlets and fry until both sides are browned and the centres set.
Keep them modest in size so they cook through without burning.
Serve with beetroot or potato salad.

title: Piernik staropolski
description: An old-Polish honey gingerbread matured for days, sometimes layered with jam.
notes: The spice mix is cinnamon, pepper, ginger and cloves.
steps: Warm honey with sugar, cool slightly, then mix with flour, spice, eggs and soda.
Rest the dough overnight if you can.
Bake in a tin at 160°C until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool, wrap, and mature several days.
Slice thin; optional jam layers go between split slabs.

title: Kutia-style wheat dessert
description: Wheat berries cooked until tender, mixed with poppy seeds, honey and nuts — an eastern Polish Christmas Eve sweet.
notes: Pearl barley is a last-resort swap; the chew will differ.
steps: Simmer wheat berries until they burst and are tender; drain.
Scald poppy seeds, drain, and grind them until they release milk.
Mix wheat with poppy, honey, chopped walnuts, raisins and enough milk to loosen.
Chill; kutia is served cool.
It should be spoonable, not dry like granola.

title: Bigos
description: Hunter's stew of sauerkraut, fresh cabbage, mixed meats and dried mushroom, cooked until the pot tastes like one thing.
notes: A Christmas meat-day dish, not a Wigilia fast dish.
steps: Brown pork, then add sausage, chopped cabbages, soaked mushrooms and prunes.
Add a little water and simmer at least three hours, stirring so it does not catch.
The stew is ready when the cabbage is mahogany and the meats yield.
Cool and reheat at least once; bigos is better on day two.
Serve with rye bread.

title: Pierogi with cabbage and mushroom
description: Boiled dumplings filled with sauerkraut and mushrooms, the Christmas Eve pierogi.
notes: Dry filling is the difference between dumplings and explosions.
steps: Cook sauerkraut and chopped mushrooms with onion until dry; cool.
Make dough with flour, egg, salt and water; roll and cut rounds.
Fill, crimp firmly, and boil until they float plus a minute.
Toss with butter.
Fry leftovers the next day until the skins blister.

title: Kompot z suszu
description: A smoky-sweet drink of dried apples, pears and prunes simmered for the Christmas Eve table.
notes: This is the Wigilia drink, not wine.
steps: Rinse the dried fruit and cover with water.
Add cinnamon and simmer until the fruit is plump and the liquor is amber, about 40 minutes.
Sweeten lightly; the fruit is already sweet.
Serve warm or at room temperature in glasses, with a few pieces of fruit in each.
It keeps two days chilled.

title: Śledzie w oleju
description: Herring fillets marinated with onion in oil, a sharp Christmas Eve fish plate.
notes: Soak very salty herring in milk first if needed.
steps: Drain herring and layer with sliced onion and bay.
Cover with oil and pepper.
Chill at least four hours, preferably overnight.
Serve with rye bread.
The onion should pickle slightly in the oil and herring brine.

title: Makowiec
description: A yeast roll swirled with ground poppy-seed filling, iced or left plain for Christmas.
notes: A paste that is too wet leaks; cook it until it holds a spoon.
steps: Make a yeast dough with flour, milk, eggs, butter and yeast; rise until doubled.
Grind scalded poppy seeds and cook briefly with honey into a thick filling; cool.
Roll the dough, spread poppy filling, and roll into a log; rise again.
Bake at 170°C until gold and cooked through.
Cool before slicing to keep the swirl.

title: Christmas sernik
description: A baked Polish cheesecake on a thin crust, dense and pale, for the sweet Christmas table.
notes: Farmer cheese beaten smooth stands in for twaróg.
steps: Make a short crust, line a tin, and blind-bake 10 minutes.
Beat twaróg with sugar, eggs and potato starch until smooth.
Pour on the crust and bake at 160°C until the centre barely wobbles.
Cool in the oven with the door ajar so the top does not crack violently.
Chill before slicing.

title: Zupa grzybowa
description: A forest mushroom soup for Christmas Eve, dark and fragrant, finished with a little cream or left lean.
notes: Skip cream for a stricter Wigilia fast.
steps: Soak porcini, then simmer them in the soaking liquor with chopped fresh mushrooms and onion.
Cook until the soup smells deeply of forest and the mushrooms are tender.
Stir in cream off the heat if using, and finish with dill.
Taste for salt; dried mushrooms vary.
Serve with noodles or on its own before the fish.

title: Kapusta z grochem
description: Sauerkraut cooked with yellow peas until both are soft — a humble Wigilia side.
notes: The dish should be moist, not swimming.
steps: Soak peas and simmer until almost tender.
Cook onion in oil, add sauerkraut and marjoram, then the peas and a little of their liquor.
Simmer until the cabbage is soft and the peas start to collapse.
Taste for salt; sauerkraut may already be enough.
Serve warm as a side to fish or mushroom cutlets.

title: Gołąbki
description: Polish cabbage rolls with pork and rice in tomato sauce — distinct from Romanian sarmale and Hungarian töltött káposzta by the sweet cabbage and tomato finish.
notes: Sweet cabbage, not pickled, is the Polish tell.
steps: Blanch a whole cabbage and peel leaves; mix pork with rice, onion and dill.
Roll, pack in a dish, and cover with passata and water.
Bake covered at 170°C until the rice is cooked and the leaves are tender.
Spoon tomato sauce over each roll.
Rest 10 minutes before serving.

title: Carp in aspic
description: Poached carp set in a clear garlic jelly, sliced cold for Christmas Eve.
notes: Heads and bones in the poaching pot help the jelly set.
steps: Poach carp with carrot, onion, bay and salt until the fish is just done; lift carefully.
Reduce the liquor, add crushed garlic, and check that a spoonful jells in the fridge.
Arrange fish and carrot slices in a dish and pour the liquor over.
Chill overnight.
Slice and serve with horseradish or vinegar.

title: Kluski śląskie
description: Silesian potato dumplings with a dimple to catch gravy, served beside roast meats on a feast day.
notes: Work while the potato is warm or the dough cracks.
steps: Rice hot boiled potatoes and mix with starch, egg and salt while warm.
Shape balls, press a dimple in each with a thumb.
Poach in salted water until they float and look slightly glassy.
Toss with butter.
Serve under gravy so the dimples fill.

title: Pierogi ruskie
description: Dumplings filled with potato and twaróg, boiled and buttered — a year-round plate that still appears at Christmas.
notes: Ruskie means Ruthenian, not Russian; the filling is potato-cheese.
steps: Mash potatoes with twaróg and fried onion for the filling; cool.
Make dough, roll, fill, and crimp.
Boil until they float plus a minute.
Toss with more butter and fried onion.
Serve with sour cream if you like.

title: Żurek
description: Sour rye soup with sausage and egg, more Easter than Christmas in some houses but a winter staple worth the pot.
notes: Bought żur concentrate works if you do not ferment rye flour at home.
steps: Simmer sausage, potato, garlic and bay in water until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in sour rye starter and heat without a hard boil.
Add halved boiled eggs to the bowls.
The soup should taste sour and garlicky.
Serve with rye bread.

title: Kluski z makiem
description: Noodles tossed with ground poppy seeds, honey and nuts — a Wigilia dessert that is not kutia.
notes: Butter in the pan is used on non-fast days.
steps: Boil noodles until just tender; drain.
Grind scalded poppy seeds and mix with honey, chopped walnuts and raisins.
Toss the hot noodles with the poppy mixture.
Serve warm or cooled.
It should look well coated, not dry.

title: Vegetarian bigos
description: Sauerkraut and mushroom stew without meat, dried fruit for depth — a Wigilia-friendly hunter's stew.
notes: Do not call it the same as meat bigos; it is a parallel dish.
steps: Cook onion in oil, add both cabbages, soaked mushrooms and prunes.
Simmer two hours until the mix is dark and concentrated.
Stir so it does not catch.
Rest overnight if you can; reheat to serve.
The mushrooms replace the smoked meat aroma.

title: Warm beetroot soup with dumpling
description: A simpler everyday beet soup with potato, thicker than clear barszcz, for a non-Eve winter lunch.
notes: Vinegar at the table lets people sharpen their own.
steps: Simmer diced beetroot, potato and onion until soft.
Mash a few cubes against the pot to thicken slightly.
Season with salt.
Serve with a spoon of sour cream and dill.
This is not the clear Christmas Eve barszcz; keep both in the book as different bowls.

title: Piernik honey cakes
description: Small honey-spice cakes baked as cookies rather than a matured loaf, for last-minute Christmas tins.
notes: Not a substitute for aged piernik loaf, but the same spice in a cookie.
steps: Mix honey, sugar, egg, flour, spice and soda into a soft dough.
Scoop small mounds onto a tray.
Bake at 170°C until puffed and just firm.
Cool; they soften in a tin.
A thin lemon glaze is optional.

title: Sałatka jarzynowa
description: Polish vegetable salad of potato, carrot, peas and pickle in mayonnaise — the party bowl next to herring.
notes: Related to salată de boeuf but without the beef.
steps: Boil potatoes, carrots and eggs until just done; cool and dice.
Dice pickles; keep everything in even cubes.
Fold with peas and mayonnaise.
Chill two hours.
Taste for pickle salt before adding more.

title: Carp Jewish-style
description: Carp simmered with onion and raisins in a sweet-sour sauce, a Polish-Jewish Christmas Eve variant.
notes: Chill and serve cold in some houses; hot is also correct.
steps: Cook onion until soft, add raisins, sugar, vinegar and a little water.
Nestle carp portions in the sauce and simmer until the fish just flakes.
Taste for a balance of sweet and sour.
Serve with the onions spooned over.
Do not boil hard or the fish breaks.

title: Barszcz with krokiety
description: Clear beet broth served with fried pancakes rolled around cabbage-mushroom filling — a Kraków café pairing at home.
notes: Use leftover uszka filling if you have it.
steps: Cook sauerkraut with mushrooms until dry for the filling.
Make thin pancakes from flour, eggs and milk; cook them pale.
Roll filling in each pancake, bread if you like, and fry until crisp.
Heat beet broth separately so it stays clear.
Serve krokiety beside a cup of barszcz, not swimming in it.

title: Mini poppy seed rolls
description: Small makowiec spirals baked as cookies for a mixed Polish sweet plate.
notes: Easier to gift than a whole makowiec log.
steps: Make a small yeast dough; rise.
Cook ground poppy with honey into a thick filling.
Roll, spread, roll up, and cut into spirals.
Bake at 180°C until gold.
Cool so the filling sets.

title: Mushroom soup with łazanki
description: Mushroom soup bulked with square noodles for a Christmas Eve supper that is more meal than cup.
notes: Any small pasta square works if łazanki are missing.
steps: Simmer soaked mushrooms and onion until the broth is dark.
Cook łazanki separately, then combine.
Stir in butter and parsley.
The pasta should be coated, not drowning, unless you want a thinner soup.
Taste for salt after the pasta goes in.

title: Pierogi with dried plum
description: Sweet pierogi filled with stewed prunes, dusted with sugar or buttered breadcrumbs.
notes: A Wigilia dessert that is not poppy seed.
steps: Stew prunes with a little water and sugar until they mash; cool.
Make dough, fill small pierogi, and boil until they float.
Brown breadcrumbs in butter.
Toss the dumplings in the crumbs.
Serve warm as a sweet course.

title: Herring in cream
description: Herring with apple, onion and sour cream — a milder Christmas Eve fish than oil-only śledzie.
notes: Pat herring dry so the cream does not go watery.
steps: Slice herring, apple and onion.
Fold with sour cream and a pinch of sugar.
Chill at least an hour so the dressing thickens around the herring.
Serve with bread.
The apple should stay crisp, so dress close to serving if you cut it early.

title: Turrón-style almond nougat
description: A hard almond nougat cooked to a brittle honey paste, pressed into a slab and cut into bars — original TDG method, not a factory copy.
notes: Aim for a snap, not a chew; that is the Alicante style in this version.
steps: Toast almonds until they smell sweet and keep them warm.
Cook honey and sugar until the syrup reaches a firm ball, then fold into a stiff egg white with lemon zest.
Work in the almonds quickly and press the mass into a lined tin.
Cool completely, then cut with an oiled knife.
Store airtight; humidity turns brittle turrón sticky.

title: Soft Jijona-style turrón
description: A softer almond nougat ground until oily and pressed into a crumbly slab, distinct from the hard bar.
notes: Do not swap this with the hard turrón on the same tasting note; they are a pair.
steps: Toast almonds and grind them until they turn into a coarse butter.
Cook honey and sugar, fold into whipped egg white, then beat in the almond paste and cinnamon.
Press into a tin and cool until sliceable but still tender.
The texture should crumble, not shatter.
Wrap well; it dries at the edges.

title: Polvorones
description: Andalusian shortbread crumbs of lard, flour and almond, baked pale and wrapped in paper so they explode into powder.
notes: Butter works if you skip lard, but the flavour shifts.
steps: Toast flour in a dry pan until it smells nutty; cool.
Rub in lard, almonds, icing sugar and cinnamon to a dough that just holds.
Cut thick ovals and bake at 160°C until the edges barely colour.
Cool completely before lifting; they are fragile.
Wrap in tissue; the crumb should melt on the tongue.

title: Mantecados
description: Soft Andalusian Christmas cakes related to polvorones but rounder and often cinnamon-heavy.
notes: They should compress, not snap.
steps: Toast the flour, then mix with lard, sugar, cinnamon and lemon zest.
Shape thick rounds.
Bake at 160°C until set but still pale.
Cool on the tray so they do not crumble in your hands.
Dust with extra cinnamon if you like a darker look.

title: Bacalao al pil-pil
description: Salt cod gently cooked in olive oil while the pan is swirled to make an emulsion from the fish gelatin.
notes: Low heat is the entire trick; boiling oil will never emulsify.
steps: Soak salt cod 24 hours, changing water; pat dry and check for bones.
Warm oil with garlic and chilli, then cook the cod skin-side down on low heat.
Tilt and swirl the pan so the oil and fish juices emulsify into a white sauce.
The fish should flake but stay in one piece.
Serve with the pil-pil spooned over; bread is required.

title: Roscón de Reyes
description: A scented Epiphany ring bread decorated with candied fruit, sliced for the twelfth-night table and often eaten through Christmas week.
notes: Orange blossom should perfume, not taste soapy — a little is enough.
steps: Make a rich yeast dough with flour, milk, butter, eggs, yeast and orange blossom water; rise until doubled.
Shape into a ring, decorate with candied fruit, and rise again.
Bake at 180°C until gold and hollow-sounding.
Cool, then split and fill with cream if you want the pastelería version.
Hide a bean or figurine only if guests know the game.

title: Pestiños
description: Anise-scented fried pastry folds dipped in honey, a southern Spanish Christmas sweet.
notes: Wine in the dough is traditional and cooks off in the fryer.
steps: Warm oil with anise, then mix with wine and flour into a dough; rest 30 minutes.
Roll thin, cut squares, and fold two corners to the centre.
Fry until blistered and gold; drain.
Dip in warm honey and sprinkle sesame.
Let them dry on a rack so they are sticky, not soggy.

title: Mazapán de Toledo
description: Toledo marzipan shaped into simple figures and baked just until the edges blush.
notes: Do not overbake or they turn into amaretti.
steps: Knead almonds, icing sugar, egg white and lemon into a smooth paste.
Shape into small figures or simple balls.
Bake at 180°C just until the ridges colour.
Brush with a little sugar syrup if you want shine.
Cool; they keep well in a tin.

title: Vino caliente
description: Spanish hot wine with orange and cinnamon, simpler and often less sweet than northern mulled wines.
notes: A young tempranillo is enough.
steps: Warm wine with orange slices, cinnamon, star anise and sugar.
Keep it below a boil for 12 minutes.
Taste; Spanish table wine needs less sugar than German market cups.
Strain into glasses.
Serve with polvorones, not sausages.

title: Christmas roast lamb
description: Castilian roast lamb with garlic and water in the tin so the meat steams then browns — a Christmas main in inland Spain.
notes: Suckling lamb is traditional in Castilla; shoulder is the practical home cut.
steps: Rub lamb with oil, salt, sliced garlic and rosemary.
Roast in a tin with water at 180°C, topping up if it dries, until the meat yields.
Raise heat at the end to brown the fat.
Rest 20 minutes.
The tin juices are the sauce; do not thicken them with flour.

title: Christmas seafood rice
description: A festive rice with mixed seafood, cooked in a wide pan until the bottom catches slightly.
notes: This is not a weekday paella shortcut; use proper stock.
steps: Sauté tomato, add rice and saffron, then fish stock.
Simmer without stirring much, nestling prawns and mussels in as the rice cooks.
Listen for the crackle that means a crust is forming.
Rest five minutes off the heat under a cloth.
Discard any mussels that stay shut.

title: Rabanadas
description: Portuguese Christmas french toast: stale bread soaked in spiced milk, fried, and dusted with cinnamon sugar.
notes: Use dense bread; sandwich slices fall apart.
steps: Warm milk with some sugar and cinnamon; soak bread slices until they drink but hold together.
Dip in beaten egg and fry in butter until both sides are gold.
Dust with remaining cinnamon sugar.
Serve warm; they soften if they sit.
A drizzle of honey is common in some houses.

title: Bolo Rei
description: A Portuguese king cake ring studded with nuts and candied fruit, baked for Christmas and Kings' Day.
notes: The dried fava bean tradition is optional; warn guests if you include one.
steps: Make a rich yeast dough; knead in most of the fruit and walnuts, saving some for the top.
Shape into a ring, decorate, and rise until puffy.
Bake at 180°C until gold and cooked through.
Brush with a light syrup while warm so the fruit shines.
Cool before slicing; the crumb is tender.

title: Bacalhau com natas
description: Salt cod baked with fried potatoes and cream — a richer Portuguese Christmas bacalhau than the boiled versions.
notes: Do not skip soaking or the dish will be inedibly salty.
steps: Soak the bacalhau, then flake it off the bones.
Fry potato cubes and onion in oil until gold.
Layer potatoes, fish and onion, pour over cream with nutmeg, and bake at 190°C until bubbling.
The top should brown in spots.
Rest five minutes so the cream thickens.

title: Bacalhau à Brás
description: Shredded salt cod scrambled with matchstick potatoes and egg, finished with parsley and olives.
notes: The eggs should be glossy, not dry like breakfast scramble.
steps: Soak and flake the bacalhau; cut potatoes into matchsticks and fry until crisp.
Soften onion in oil, add the fish, then the potatoes.
Pour in beaten eggs and scramble softly so everything binds but stays moist.
Finish with parsley.
Serve at once; leftover Brás goes sad.

title: Sonhos de Natal
description: Airy fried choux puffs rolled in cinnamon sugar — Portuguese Christmas 'dreams'.
notes: Oil that is too hot browns them before they puff.
steps: Bring water and butter to a boil, add flour, and beat into a paste off the heat.
Beat in eggs one at a time until the choux is glossy.
Fry spoonfuls in 170°C oil until they swell and gold; drain.
Toss in cinnamon sugar.
Eat the same day while they are still hollow and crisp.

title: Aletria
description: Sweet vermicelli cooked in milk with lemon and cinnamon, set into a soft Christmas pudding.
notes: Do not boil after the yolks go in.
steps: Simmer vermicelli in milk with lemon peel, sugar and cinnamon until the pasta is soft and the milk thick.
Off the heat, stir in yolks to enrich.
Pour into a dish and cool until it just sets.
Dust with more cinnamon in a pattern if you like.
Serve at room temperature.

title: Caldo verde
description: A green soup of potato and finely sliced kale with a slice of sausage — a Portuguese winter starter.
notes: Couve galega is traditional; cavolo nero is a decent stand-in.
steps: Cook potatoes with garlic in salted water until soft, then mash them into the liquor.
Slice kale into hair-thin shreds and simmer them in the potato soup until just tender.
Fry chorizo slices and add them with their oil.
Finish with olive oil at the table.
The kale should stay green, not khaki.

title: Polvo à lagareiro
description: Octopus roasted with smashed potatoes and a flood of olive oil and garlic — a Christmas Eve fish main.
notes: Frozen octopus often tenderises more reliably than cheap fresh.
steps: Simmer octopus until tender, then cut into pieces.
Parboil potatoes, smash them, and roast with oil, garlic and salt until crisp at the edges.
Add octopus to the tin and roast until the suckers colour.
Finish with parsley and more oil.
The dish should be glossy, not dry.

title: Broa de milho
description: A dense Portuguese corn-and-rye bread, sliced beside caldo verde or bacalhau.
notes: A little wheat flour can be added if the dough will not hold.
steps: Mix cornmeal, rye, yeast, salt and warm water into a sticky dough; rise 45 minutes.
Shape a round loaf without much kneading.
Bake at 200°C until the crust is dark and the loaf sounds hollow.
Cool before slicing; hot broa crumbles.
The crumb is moist and close, not airy like wheat bread.

title: Filhós
description: Orange-scented fried dough pieces, crisp outside and soft within, piled for Christmas.
notes: Irregular shapes are correct; these are not doughnuts.
steps: Make a yeast dough with flour, eggs, orange juice, zest, yeast and a little sugar; rise until puffy.
Pull irregular pieces and fry until gold.
Drain and dust with remaining sugar.
Serve piled on a platter.
They stale overnight; make them the day you eat them.

title: Arroz doce
description: Portuguese rice pudding finished with egg yolk and a cinnamon lattice on top.
notes: Stir often; milk rice catches easily.
steps: Cook rice in milk with lemon peel until creamy.
Stir in sugar, then yolks off the heat.
Pour into a dish and cool until it just sets.
Dust cinnamon in a lattice using a paper stencil or a steady hand.
Serve at room temperature.

title: Vinho quente
description: Portuguese mulled wine with orange and a strip of lemon, less spice-forward than Nordic glögg.
notes: Port in the pan makes it heavy; serve port separately if you want it.
steps: Warm wine with citrus slices, cinnamon, cloves and sugar.
Steep below a simmer 12 minutes.
Strain into glasses.
A Portuguese table wine is enough; do not use vintage port here.
Keep warm for late guests.

title: Roast bacalhau with broa crumb
description: Loins of soaked salt cod roasted under a garlic olive-oil crumb of corn bread.
notes: Any dense corn bread can stand in for broa.
steps: Soak and drain the bacalhau; lay it on onion slices in a tin.
Crumble broa with garlic, parsley and oil, then pack it on the fish.
Roast at 190°C until the crumb is crisp and the fish flakes.
Spoon pan oil over as you serve.
A green salad cuts the richness.

title: Cinnamon polvorones
description: A cinnamon-leaning polvorón, distinct from the plainer almond version, still pale and powdery.
notes: Keep both recipes; they are not the same biscuit.
steps: Toast flour, cool, and rub in lard, almonds, sugar and extra cinnamon.
Cut thick ovals.
Bake at 160°C until barely coloured.
Cool fully before moving.
They should perfume more of cinnamon than the almond polvorones.

title: Chocolate almond turrón bar
description: A home chocolate turrón slab with roasted almonds, set in a tin rather than pulled as nougat.
notes: This is an original TDG bar inspired by Spanish Christmas chocolate turrón, not a branded copy.
steps: Toast almonds and chop them coarsely.
Melt chocolate with butter and honey, then stir in almonds and salt.
Spread in a lined tin and chill until firm.
Cut the set slab into bars with a warm knife.
Keep cool; it is closer to a mendiant slab than classic nougat.

title: Gambas al ajillo
description: Prawns seared in a pool of garlic olive oil with chilli — a Christmas Eve tapa that takes minutes.
notes: Head-on prawns flavour the oil more; peeled are easier for a crowd.
steps: Warm oil with sliced garlic and chilli until the garlic just turns gold.
Add prawns and cook until they curl and turn opaque.
Salt and finish with parsley.
Serve in the pan with bread.
Do not walk away; garlic burns in seconds.

title: Ensaimada de Mallorca
description: A coiled lard-laminated breakfast pastry from Mallorca, dusted with sugar, for a slow Christmas morning.
notes: Butter can replace lard with a different flavour.
steps: Make a soft yeast dough with flour, eggs, sugar, yeast and water; rest until doubled.
Roll very thin, smear with lard, roll into a rope, and coil in a round tin.
Rise until very puffy.
Bake at 180°C until gold, then dust heavily with sugar.
Pull apart with your hands; a knife squashes the layers.

title: Seafood Christmas broth
description: A clearish Galician-style broth of fish bones, onion and parsley to start a Christmas Eve fish meal.
notes: Prawn heads in the pot add sweetness.
steps: Cover bones with water, add onion, leek, bay and salt, and simmer 40 minutes, skimming.
Strain through cloth.
Finish with parsley.
Serve in cups before the main fish.
Do not boil or the broth goes cloudy and bitter.

title: Bolo Rainha
description: The nut-heavy sister of bolo rei, without candied fruit on top, baked as a Christmas ring.
notes: Keep both cakes if you are feeding a mixed Portuguese table.
steps: Make a rich yeast dough and knead in most of the walnuts and pine nuts.
Shape a ring, stud with remaining nuts, and rise.
Bake at 180°C until cooked through.
Cool, then slice.
It is less jewelled than bolo rei and more toasted-nut in flavour.

title: Clams Bulhão Pato
description: Clams steamed with garlic, coriander and lemon — a Lisbon starter that fits a Christmas Eve seafood spread.
notes: Coriander is the Portuguese tell; parsley is a different dish.
steps: Purge clams in salted water, then rinse.
Warm oil with garlic, add clams and wine, and cover until they open.
Finish with chopped coriander and lemon juice.
Discard any that stay shut.
Serve with bread for the liquor.

title: Migas extremeñas
description: Fried breadcrumbs with garlic and pepper, a shepherd breakfast that uses leftover Christmas bread.
notes: The bread must be stale; fresh bread fries into greasy sponge.
steps: Sprinkle bread cubes with a little water so they soften without going soggy.
Fry garlic and chorizo in oil, then add bread and paprika.
Cook, stirring, until the crumbs are unevenly crisp.
Salt and serve hot.
A fried grape or two on top is a regional flourish if you have them.

title: Portuguese garlic soup
description: A bread-thickened garlic broth with egg, eaten as a restoring Christmas-week supper or late breakfast.
notes: Coriander is a common finish in Alentejo.
steps: Fry garlic in oil until gold, add water and salt, and simmer 10 minutes.
Add bread to thicken.
Poach eggs in the soup or stir beaten egg for ribbons.
Serve immediately.
The soup should taste loudly of garlic and olive oil.

title: Yolk turrón cream bars
description: A soft turrón enriched with egg yolk, set into bars that slice rather than shatter.
notes: Original TDG method inspired by turrón de yema quemada, without a blowtorched top.
steps: Cook sugar and honey to a thick syrup, then beat into yolks.
Fold in almonds and cinnamon to a paste.
Press into a tin and chill until sliceable.
Cut with a wet knife.
Keep refrigerated; this style is perishable.

title: Lacón con grelos
description: Cured pork shoulder simmered with turnip greens and potatoes — a Galician winter feast plate.
notes: Kale stands in for grelos if turnip greens are missing.
steps: Soak the lacón if very salty, then simmer until tender.
Add potatoes and chorizo, then the greens for the last 15 minutes.
Slice the meat and arrange with vegetables.
Spoon a little cooking liquor over the platter.
Serve with good bread, not sauce.

title: Baked rabanadas
description: An oven version of rabanadas for feeding a crowd without standing at the frying pan.
notes: Closer to a bread pudding than the fried original; keep both.
steps: Arrange bread in a buttered dish.
Whisk milk, eggs, sugar and cinnamon, pour over, and soak 20 minutes.
Bake at 180°C until puffed and gold.
Dust with more cinnamon sugar.
Serve warm from the dish.

title: Risgrynsgröt
description: Swedish Christmas rice porridge cooked slowly in milk, served with cinnamon sugar and a hidden almond for luck.
notes: A knob of butter on each serving is traditional.
steps: Rinse rice and simmer with milk and salt on the lowest heat, stirring often, until creamy, about 50 minutes.
Sweeten lightly.
Hide one almond in the pot.
Serve in bowls with cinnamon sugar.
The finder of the almond is supposed to marry next year, or at least do the washing-up.

title: Glögg
description: Swedish mulled wine with cardamom, ginger, raisins and almonds in the cup — spicier and fruitier than plain mulled wine.
notes: Cardamom is the Swedish tell; do not skip it.
steps: Warm wine with crushed cardamom, ginger and cinnamon; do not boil.
Steep 15 minutes, then strain.
Put raisins and almonds in each cup before pouring.
Sweeten to taste with sugar if the wine is very dry.
A splash of vodka or rum is optional for a stronger glögg.

title: Pepparkakor
description: Thin Swedish ginger snaps cut into hearts and pigs, baked until they snap.
notes: Thin rolling is more important than extra spice.
steps: Warm butter with sugar and syrup, then mix into flour and spices; chill the dough.
Roll very thin, cut shapes, and bake at 200°C for 6–8 minutes until the edges darken.
Cool on the tray so they crisp.
They should snap, not bend.
Hang a few with ribbon if you cut a hole before baking.

title: Gravlax with mustard sauce
description: Salmon cured with salt, sugar and dill until it slices like silk, served with a sweet mustard sauce.
notes: Use a centre-cut fillet without too many pin bones.
steps: Mix salt and sugar, rub over the salmon, and pack dill on both sides.
Wrap, weight, and cure in the fridge 48 hours, turning once.
Rinse lightly, pat dry, and slice thinly at an angle.
Stir mustard with honey and chopped dill for a sauce.
Serve with rye or boiled potatoes.

title: Janssons frestelse
description: A creamy potato gratin with sprats or anchovy-style sprats — the Swedish Christmas table's salty temptation.
notes: Swedish ansjovis (sprats) are not Mediterranean anchovies; use sprats in brine if you can.
steps: Cut potatoes into matchsticks and slice onion.
Layer potatoes, onion and sprats in a buttered dish, salting lightly.
Pour over cream and dot with butter.
Bake at 200°C until the top is brown and the potatoes are tender.
Rest 10 minutes so it sets enough to spoon.

title: Julskinka
description: Swedish Christmas ham poached then roasted with a mustard-breadcrumb crust.
notes: Swedish ham is often eaten cold on Christmas Day after a Christmas Eve roast.
steps: Poach the ham with onion until heated through and tender, about 90 minutes.
Peel the rind, score fat, and spread mustard mixed with sugar.
Press on breadcrumbs and stud with a few cloves.
Roast at 220°C until the crust is gold.
Serve warm or cold with mustard.

title: Kåldolmar
description: Swedish cabbage rolls with pork and rice, baked in cream — related to but milder than Hungarian stuffed cabbage.
notes: Distinct from sarmale (pickled cabbage) and töltött káposzta (paprika).
steps: Blanch cabbage leaves; mix pork with cooked rice and onion.
Roll, pack in a dish, and pour over cream mixed with a little syrup.
Bake at 180°C until the rolls are cooked and the sauce is bubbling.
The syrup is a Swedish touch, not a dessert sauce.
Serve with boiled potatoes and lingonberries if you have them.

title: Lussekatter
description: Saffron buns twisted into S-shapes with raisins, baked for Lucia and eaten through Advent.
notes: Do not use food colouring instead of saffron.
steps: Bloom saffron in warm milk, then make a yeast dough with flour, butter, sugar, egg and yeast.
Rise, then shape S-shaped cats with a raisin in each curve.
Prove again, egg-wash, and bake at 200°C until gold.
Eat the same day; they dry fast.
Proper saffron should colour the dough yolk-yellow.

title: Inlagd sill
description: Pickled herring in a sweet-sour onion brine, a cornerstone of the Swedish Christmas table.
notes: Bought pickled herring can be refreshed in this brine.
steps: Soak herring if very salty, then cut into pieces.
Boil vinegar, sugar, bay and allspice, then cool the brine.
Layer herring and onion, pour brine over, and chill overnight.
Serve with boiled potatoes and sour cream.
The onion should pickle until translucent.

title: Knäck
description: Swedish Christmas toffee with almonds, cooked to a chewy set and poured into paper cases.
notes: A thermometer to about 125°C gives the classic chew.
steps: Cook sugar, syrup and cream to a firm ball stage, stirring so it does not scorch.
Stir in butter and chopped almonds.
Pour into small paper cases.
Cool until the knäck is chewy, not rock-hard, unless you cooked it further.
Store cool and dry.

title: Vörtbröd
description: A dark Swedish wort bread with raisins and spices, sliced for Christmas breakfast with ham.
notes: Beer stands in for brewing wort in a home kitchen.
steps: Mix flours with beer, yeast, spice, salt and raisins into a sticky dough; rise 60 minutes.
Shape a loaf and rise again.
Bake at 190°C until the crust is dark and the loaf sounds hollow.
Cool before slicing.
The crumb should be moist and fragrant with spice.

title: Swedish Christmas meatballs
description: Small pork-beef meatballs in a cream gravy, a julbord essential rather than an Ikea joke.
notes: Keep them small; large ones belong to another cuisine.
steps: Mix meats with soaked breadcrumbs, egg and salt; roll small balls.
Brown in batches, then deglaze with stock.
Stir in cream and simmer the meatballs until cooked through.
The gravy should be pale and savoury.
Serve with lingonberry jam and potatoes.

title: Swedish red cabbage
description: Red cabbage cooked with apple and a little redcurrant jelly, milder than German clove-heavy rotkohl.
notes: Intentionally distinct from German and Danish red cabbage recipes in this catalog.
steps: Shred cabbage and apple and cook with vinegar, salt and allspice until tender.
Stir in jelly at the end for gloss and fruit.
The spice should be background, not a clove bomb.
It reheats well the next day without losing the apple sweetness.
Serve with ham or meatballs.

title: Ribbe
description: Norwegian pork belly roasted so the crackling blisters into squares — the eastern Christmas centrepiece.
notes: Dry skin is the crackling secret; pat it obsessively.
steps: Score the pork skin in a tight grid, rub with salt, and refrigerate uncovered overnight if you can.
Set on onions in a tin with water and roast at 160°C until the meat is tender.
Blast at 230°C until the crackling puffs and blisters.
Rest 20 minutes, then cut along the scores.
Serve with surkål and potatoes.

title: Pinnekjøtt
description: Salted dried lamb ribs steamed over birch sticks until the meat yields — western Norway's Christmas plate.
notes: Bought cured ribs are the realistic home option.
steps: Soak pinnekjøtt overnight to temper the salt.
Steam over a rack (birch sticks if you have them) above simmering water for three hours until tender.
Boil potatoes and swede separately.
Mash swede with a little of the steaming liquor if it is not too salty.
Serve the ribs whole; people pick the meat.

title: Surkål
description: Norwegian sweet-sour cabbage with caraway, the classic partner to ribbe.
notes: Caraway is the Norwegian note; skip cloves.
steps: Shred cabbage and cook with vinegar, sugar, caraway, salt and water until tender but not mush.
Taste for a clear sweet-sour balance.
It should stay pale, not brown.
Reheat gently beside the pork.
Make it the day before if you can.

title: Medisterkaker
description: Large Norwegian pork patties spiced with ginger and nutmeg, browned and simmered in gravy.
notes: They should be plump, not smashed thin like burgers.
steps: Mix pork with breadcrumbs, egg, ginger, nutmeg, salt and enough milk to make a soft mince.
Shape large flat cakes and brown on both sides.
Simmer in a little stock or water until cooked through.
Reduce the pan juices into a light gravy.
Serve with ribbe leftovers or as the main for a smaller table.

title: Peppernøtter
description: Small Norwegian pepper cookies, harder than pepparkakor, meant for a tin that lasts Advent.
notes: Smaller than a walnut; they are nibble cookies.
steps: Beat butter and sugar, add egg, then flour, pepper, cinnamon and soda.
Roll small balls and bake at 180°C until they feel dry.
They harden as they cool.
Store in a tin for a week; they mellow.
White pepper should be noticeable.

title: Lefse with butter and sugar
description: Soft potato flatbreads griddled, then spread with butter and sugar and folded — a Christmas-week breakfast.
notes: The potatoes must be dry and cold or the dough sticks.
steps: Rice cold boiled potatoes and mix with flour and salt into a dough.
Roll thin rounds and cook on a dry griddle until spotted.
Spread with butter and sugar while warm, then fold.
Keep stacked under a cloth so they stay supple.
Eat the same day.

title: Lutefisk with peas and bacon
description: Lye-treated cod baked until translucent, served with pea stew and bacon — polarising and traditional.
notes: Buy prepared lutefisk; do not make lye fish from scratch at home.
steps: Soak and cook peas into a thick stew; boil potatoes; fry bacon until crisp.
Bake lutefisk covered at 200°C until it turns translucent and just flakes; salt lightly.
The fish should not brown.
Plate with peas, potatoes and bacon.
Have melted butter on the table.

title: Norwegian risengrynsgrøt
description: Norwegian Christmas rice porridge, cousin to the Swedish pot, often eaten for lunch on Christmas Eve before the savoury meal.
notes: Same family as risgrynsgröt; this pot is slightly less sweet as a lunch.
steps: Cook rice in milk with salt until thick and tender.
Sweeten to taste.
Hide one whole almond in the pot before you ladle the porridge.
Serve with cinnamon sugar and butter.
Leftovers become riskrem the next day if you fold in whipped cream.

title: Flæskesteg
description: Danish roast pork with a scored rind that becomes crackling, served with red cabbage and caramel potatoes.
notes: The rind must be dry and heavily salted.
steps: Score the rind down to the fat, rub salt into every cut, and tuck bay into a few scores.
Roast at 160°C with water in the tin until the meat is done, then raise heat to blister the rind.
Rest 20 minutes.
Carve so each slice has a strip of crackling.
Use tin juices for a simple gravy.

title: Brunede kartofler
description: Small potatoes caramelised in sugar and butter until they shine like toffee — a Danish Christmas side.
notes: Waxy small potatoes hold together; large floury ones break.
steps: Boil potatoes in skins, peel while warm, and dry them.
Melt sugar in a wide pan until amber, then add butter.
Tumble in potatoes and salt, turning until every one is coated and browned.
Work quickly so the caramel does not burn.
Serve immediately; they dull as they cool.

title: Risalamande
description: Cold rice pudding folded with whipped cream and almonds, served with cherry sauce, and one whole almond hidden.
notes: The rice must be cold before the cream goes in or it weeps.
steps: Cook rice in milk until thick; cool completely.
Whip cream and fold it into the rice with chopped almonds, hiding one whole almond.
Simmer cherries with sugar into a loose sauce.
Serve the cold pudding with warm cherry sauce.
The almond-finder wins a small prize in many houses.

title: Æbleskiver
description: Spherical pancake puffs cooked in a dimpled pan, dusted with sugar and served with jam.
notes: A takoyaki pan is a workable substitute.
steps: Separate eggs, make a batter with yolks, flour, buttermilk and soda, then fold in whipped whites.
Heat an æbleskive pan, butter the hollows, and fill them.
Turn with a skewer when the bases set, until each ball is gold all over.
Dust with sugar and serve with jam.
Keep the pan hot or they stick.

title: Rødkål
description: Danish red cabbage cooked with vinegar and currant juice, the required partner to flæskesteg.
notes: Redcurrant juice is the Danish tell versus apple-only German pots.
steps: Shred cabbage and apple, then cook with vinegar, juice, sugar and salt until silky.
The flavour should be sweet-sour, not clove-heavy.
Make it a day ahead.
Reheat without boiling away the gloss.
Serve with pork and caramel potatoes.

title: Kransekake
description: Stacked almond rings forming a tower, iced with white lines — a celebration cake for New Year and Christmas parties.
notes: Special ring tins help; freeform rings work if you size them carefully.
steps: Mix almonds, icing sugar and egg whites into a paste; rest an hour.
Pipe or roll rings in graduated sizes.
Bake at 180°C until they just take colour.
Cool, then stack with royal icing as glue, piping zigzags.
The tower should be crisp-chewy, not dry.

title: Danish gløgg
description: Danish mulled wine with snaps optional, raisins and almonds in the cup, close to Swedish glögg but often sweeter.
notes: Sweeter than the French vin chaud in this catalog.
steps: Warm wine with cinnamon, cloves and sugar.
Steep 15 minutes below a boil.
Put raisins and almonds in cups, then pour.
A spoon of snaps is optional for adults.
Do not confuse with alcohol-free gløgg for children; make a separate juice pot.

title: Andesteg
description: Danish roast duck stuffed with apple and prune, a Christmas bird for households that skip pork.
notes: Prunes in the cavity are the Danish signature here.
steps: Salt the duck, stuff with apple, prunes and thyme, and set in a tin with water.
Roast at 160°C, pouring off fat, until the thighs are done.
Raise heat to crisp the skin.
Rest 20 minutes; spoon the fruit out as garnish.
Serve with rødkål and potatoes.

title: Klejner
description: Twisted fried cookies dusted with sugar, a Danish Christmas tin staple.
notes: Cardamom should be present but not soapy.
steps: Make a firm dough with flour, butter, sugar, egg, cream and cardamom; chill.
Roll, cut diamonds, slash the centre, and pull one end through to twist.
Fry in 170°C oil until gold; drain.
Dust with sugar.
They keep a few days in a tin.

title: Pebernødder
description: Tiny Danish pepper nuts, baked hard, for filling small bags and tins.
notes: Smaller than Norwegian peppernøtter in this catalog.
steps: Mix a stiff dough, roll into thin ropes, and cut pea-sized pieces.
Bake at 180°C until dry and lightly coloured.
Cool; they should be hard enough to rattle in a tin.
Pepper and cardamom share the aroma.
Make a double batch; they vanish.

title: Brun sovs
description: Danish brown gravy from pork pan juices, slightly sweet, for flæskesteg and potatoes.
notes: A drop of gravy browning is used in some houses; better to reduce properly.
steps: Make a roux with butter and flour, then whisk in juices and stock.
Simmer until glossy.
Whisk in jelly and salt.
Strain if lumpy.
It should taste of pork, not flour.

title: Riskrem
description: Norwegian leftover rice porridge folded with whipped cream and served with raspberry sauce.
notes: Do not re-boil the porridge once cream is in.
steps: Whip cream and fold into cold porridge with a hidden almond if you like the game.
Cook raspberries with sugar into a sharp sauce.
Serve the cream-rice cold with warm sauce.
It should be fluffy, not a brick.
This is how risengrynsgrøt is reinvented on Christmas Day.

title: Mustard sauce for pinnekjøtt
description: A sharp mustard-cream sauce for steamed lamb ribs, for tables that want more than swede mash.
notes: Wholegrain mustard can replace Dijon for more texture.
steps: Stir mustard with cream, sugar, vinegar and salt.
Warm gently without boiling so it does not split.
Taste; it should cut the salt of the lamb.
Serve in a small jug.
Make it just before plating.

title: Alcohol-free glögg
description: Blackcurrant and orange juice mulled with the same spices as glögg, for children and drivers.
notes: This is not watered-down wine; start from juice.
steps: Warm juices with cinnamon, cardamom and orange slices; do not boil.
Steep 12 minutes.
Put raisins in cups and pour.
Taste; some juices need no extra sugar.
Keep a separate pot from the wine glögg so spices are not confused.

title: Mustard herring
description: Herring in a thick sweet mustard dressing, another julbord herring distinct from the onion pickle.
notes: Keep this separate from inlagd sill on the buffet.
steps: Pat herring dry.
Whisk mustard, sugar, oil and salt into a thick dressing; fold in dill.
Coat the herring and chill overnight.
Serve from a small dish with a spoon.
The dressing should cling, not pool.

title: Leverpostej
description: Danish liver pâté baked in a tin, eaten hot on Christmas morning or cold on rye all week.
notes: A food processor is kinder than a mincer for home batches.
steps: Blend liver, fat, onion, eggs, milk and flour until fairly smooth; season well.
Pour into a buttered tin and bake in a water bath at 170°C until set.
Serve a spoon hot with mushrooms, or chill and slice.
The texture should be spreadable, not a dense brick.
It keeps several days.

title: Rømmegrøt
description: A sour-cream porridge cooked until butter separates, served with cinnamon sugar — a festive Norwegian farm dessert.
notes: If you cannot get proper high-fat sour cream, the butter will not separate as dramatically.
steps: Cook sour cream slowly until the butterfat begins to separate; skim some butter to a jug.
Stir in milk and semolina and cook until thick.
Season with salt.
Serve with cinnamon sugar and the reserved butter poured over.
It is rich; small bowls are enough.

title: Swede mash for pinnekjøtt
description: Mashed swede with butter, the required yellow heap beside steamed lamb ribs.
notes: Called kålrabistappe in Norwegian kitchens.
steps: Peel and cube swede, then boil until completely soft.
Mash with butter, milk, salt and pepper until slightly rustic.
It should be buttery, not watery.
Keep warm; it sits well under a lid.
A potato or two mashed in is allowed if the swede is very strong.

title: Spiced apple Christmas cup
description: A non-cola festive cup of apple juice, ginger and cloves for a Swedish-style children's glass.
notes: Keep it off the wine glögg tray so children do not mix glasses.
steps: Warm apple juice with ginger, cloves, cinnamon and a strip of lemon.
Steep 10 minutes; do not boil.
Strain into glasses.
Serve it warm, not piping, so the flavours stay clear.
This is an original TDG juice cup, not a branded Swedish soda.

title: Mustard for lutefisk
description: A sweet-hot mustard to cut the mildness of lutefisk, stirred in a cup at the last minute.
notes: Norwegian Christmas mustard is often sweeter than French Dijon neat.
steps: Stir mustard with sugar, vinegar, water and salt until smooth.
Let it stand five minutes so the sugar dissolves.
Taste; it should be sweeter than steak mustard.
Serve in a small bowl.
Make fresh; it dulls in the fridge.

title: Gravlax smørbrød
description: Open rye sandwiches with gravlax, mustard sauce and dill — a Boxing Day breakfast from leftover cure.
notes: Uses leftover gravlax from the Eve platter.
steps: Stir mustard with honey.
Spread rye with the sauce, layer gravlax, and add dill.
Serve open, not closed.
A grind of pepper is enough.
Do not toast the rye to charcoal; just slice it.

title: Danish gingerbread slabs
description: A sturdy pepper-ginger dough baked as slabs for decorating or eating as thick biscuits.
notes: Not the Swedish thin snap; this is a decorating biscuit.
steps: Mix a stiff dough, chill, and roll 6 mm thick.
Cut slabs or simple shapes.
Bake at 180°C until the edges firm.
Cool before icing.
Thicker than pepparkakor so children can decorate without snapping every piece.

title: Potatoes cooked in lamb steam
description: Potatoes steamed under the pinnekjøtt so they pick up a little lamb perfume.
notes: Taste the steaming liquid before you commit the potatoes to it.
steps: Set potatoes in the steamer liquor under the lamb ribs, with bay and salt.
Cook until a knife slides through.
Toss with butter.
They will taste faintly of lamb; that is the point.
If the liquor is very salty, cook the potatoes in fresh water instead.

title: Port-laced glögg
description: A richer glögg finished with a little port, for a late Christmas-eve pot after dinner.
notes: Distinct from the standard glögg recipe by the port finish.
steps: Warm wine with cardamom and cinnamon; do not boil.
Add port off the heat so it stays round.
Strain into cups with raisins and almonds.
Serve in small glasses; it is stronger than breakfast glögg.
Keep the spices out after 15 minutes or they turn bitter.

title: Agurksalat
description: Quick pickled cucumber salad, sharp and sweet, to cut Danish roast pork.
notes: Do not make it hours ahead or the cucumber weeps into limpness.
steps: Slice cucumbers thinly.
Dissolve sugar and salt in vinegar, then pour over the cucumbers.
Add dill and chill 20 minutes.
Drain slightly before serving so the plate is not flooded.
They should stay crisp.

title: Brown sauce for ribbe
description: A pan gravy for Norwegian pork belly, made from roasting juices and a little cream.
notes: The crackling stays separate; this sauce is for the meat and cabbage.
steps: Skim excess fat from ribbe juices, leaving a spoon.
Cook flour in that fat, then whisk in juices, stock and cream.
Simmer until the sauce coats a spoon.
Season with salt.
Strain into a jug.

title: Julekake
description: A Norwegian Christmas bread with raisins, candied peel and cardamom, toasted for breakfast.
notes: Stale slices make excellent toast on the 27th.
steps: Make a yeast dough with flour, milk, butter, cardamom and yeast; knead in raisins and peel.
Rise, shape a round loaf, and rise again.
Bake at 180°C until gold and hollow-sounding.
Cool, then slice and butter.
Cardamom should perfume the crumb.

title: Rice porridge tart
description: Leftover Christmas rice porridge baked in a pastry case with egg until set — a TDG leftover pudding.
notes: An original leftover recipe, not a classic named cake.
steps: Line a tin with pastry and prick the base.
